Southwell
SUTH-ul
n. (the Nottinghamshire minster of the archbishops of York, a collegiate church made a cathedral in 1884)
Old English suth well, the south spring; the local pronunciation keeps the older form.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Southwell is a small town in Nottinghamshire whose minster was given to the archbishops of York in 956 and served for nine hundred years as a collegiate church of secular canons rather than a monastery, with the archbishop's palace beside it. Its Norman nave survives whole, with two western towers and a carved tympanum; its thirteenth-century chapter house holds the finest naturalistic leaf carving in England, oak, hawthorn, maple and vine cut from life by masons who evidently went out and looked. Byron is buried at nearby Hucknall and lived at Southwell as a boy. The college was dissolved and revived, and in 1884 the minster became the cathedral of a new diocese covering Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire. The dictionary records Southwell for the carved leaves. Nobody required them and nobody could see most of them well; they were done because the men who cut them loved the work and the house it was for. Scripture does not sneer at that affection: the Psalmist says he loves the habitation of God's house, and prefers a day in the courts to a thousand elsewhere.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a habitation as a place of dwelling; honour as esteem and dignity; a court as an enclosed space before a house; a doorkeeper as one who guards an entrance; and to contain as to hold within limits.

expand to see more

HABITATION, n. Act of inhabiting; state of dwelling; place of abode; a settled dwelling; a mansion.

HONOR, n. The esteem due or paid to worth; high estimation; dignity; reverence; veneration.

COURT, n. A space enclosed, or a space before a house enclosed by a wall; an open area in a palace or temple.

DOORKEEPER, n. A porter; one who guards the entrance of a house or apartment.

CONTAIN, v.t. To hold, as a vessel; to comprehend; to comprise; to include; to restrain.

Key Scripture

Psa 26:8 — "LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth."

Psa 84:10 — "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness."

2Ch 7:16 — "For now have I chosen and sanctified this house, that my name may be there for ever: and mine eyes and mine heart shall be there perpetually."

1Ki 8:27 — "But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?"

Modern Corruption

Nottinghamshire minster of the archbishops of York, a collegiate church for nine hundred years, with England's finest naturalistic leaf carving; a cathedral since 1884.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that love for the place of worship is a scriptural affection and not a weakness. David states it without embarrassment: “LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth” (Psa 26:8), and the sons of Korah put the preference in numbers, “For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand” (Psa 84:10).

The live temptation runs in both directions, and Southwell has met both: a dissolved college whose canons had drawn revenues for generations, and a Victorian restoration that risked making the carvings the point. God himself attaches his name to a particular house, “For now have I chosen and sanctified this house, that my name may be there for ever” (2Ch 7:16); and the same king who built it asked the question that keeps the affection sober: “But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee” (1Ki 8:27). The masons cut leaves for a house whose tenant is not housed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew maon (H4583), a habitation; Hebrew kabod (H3519), honour or glory; Hebrew chatser (H2691), a court; Hebrew bachar (H0977), to choose.

expand to see more

Hebrew maon (H4583) — a dwelling, a habitation; “I have loved the habitation of thy house”, Psalm 26:8.

Hebrew kabod (H3519) — weight, honour, glory; “the place where thine honour dwelleth”, Psalm 26:8.

Hebrew chatser (H2691) — a court, an enclosure; “a day in thy courts is better than a thousand”, Psalm 84:10.

Hebrew bachar (H0977) — to choose, to select; “now have I chosen and sanctified this house”, 2 Chronicles 7:16.

Hebrew kul (H3557) — to contain, to hold; “the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee”, 1 Kings 8:27.

Usage

"“I have loved the habitation of thy house” (Psa 26:8) — why masons carved hidden leaves."

"“For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand” (Psa 84:10) — the preference, in numbers."

"“the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee” (1Ki 8:27) — what keeps the affection sober."
